headline: US judge strikes down 75-country visa ban
summary: A US federal judge ruled the State Department's suspension of immigrant visas for 75 countries patently unlawful.
display_body: A US federal judge struck down the State Department policy that had suspended immigrant visas for applicants from 75 countries, calling it "patently unlawful" on Friday 21 August. US District Judge Jeannette Vargas, sitting in Manhattan (the Southern District of New York), ruled that the freeze — announced and in effect since January 2026 — exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's authority, because federal immigration law explicitly strips the secretary of control over how consular officers process immigrant visas. "The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme," she wrote. The State Department had justified the suspension by labelling applicants from those countries — among them Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Bosnia, Albania, Pakistan and Bangladesh, plus many African, Middle Eastern and Caribbean states — as "at a high risk for becoming a public charge" (immigration-law jargon for someone judged likely to depend on government support). The suit was brought by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together, together with visa applicants and US citizens sponsoring relatives; the department did not immediately comment and can appeal.
why: This is one of the broadest court rollbacks yet of the administration's immigration drive, restoring a legal path for families across dozens of countries. It rests on a structural limit rather than a discretionary one — Congress assigned immigrant-visa processing to statute, not to the secretary's judgement — which is harder to route around than a policy the administration can simply reword.

headline: Sword attack at Swedish school kills one
summary: A bladed-weapon attack at a school in Fagersta, Sweden killed one and wounded three before police shot and arrested the suspect.
display_body: A man attacked a secondary school in Fagersta, north-west of Stockholm, with a bladed weapon on the afternoon of Friday 21 August, killing one person and wounding three others, two of them seriously, before police shot and arrested him. Police received the alarm at 14:06 and had overpowered the attacker — reportedly a former pupil of the school — by 14:16, shooting him in the leg; the injured were minors, according to Swedish public broadcaster SVT. Investigators said it was too early to name a motive and reported no sign of a second attacker. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and King Carl XVI Gustaf both expressed condolences, the king noting that "Sweden has once again been struck by an attack at a school."
why: School attacks remain rare in Sweden, but this is the deadliest since the February 2025 Örebro school shooting that killed 11 — the country's worst mass shooting — and it renews a debate about school security that Örebro had already forced onto the national agenda.

headline: Jihadists kill and abduct dozens in Nigeria
summary: Lakurawa jihadists killed and kidnapped dozens during Friday prayers in Niger State, central Nigeria.
display_body: Jihadist fighters killed and abducted dozens of people during Friday prayers on 21 August in the Borgu area of Niger State, in central Nigeria, survivors and a federal lawmaker told the AFP news agency. A survivor of the assault on the village of Dikera said the Lakurawa group — an obscure armed formation that some researchers tie to the Islamic State Sahel Province, the jihadist franchise active in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — attacked with rifles, knives and machetes; many villagers escaped only when a rival jihadist group known as Mahmuda intervened and turned on the attackers. A second village, Binzi, was also hit, and the exact toll was not known; federal deputy Jafaru Mohammed corroborated the account.
why: Mass abduction has been a signature tactic of Nigeria's 17-year jihadist insurgency since the 2014 kidnapping of hundreds of schoolgirls at Chibok; an attack of this kind in Niger State signals the Sahel's armed groups pressing further south into Nigeria's central belt, and the involvement of two rival factions points to a fragmenting, harder-to-map threat.

headline: Ständerat delays EU electricity accord to winter
summary: The Council of States energy committee postponed its Swiss-EU electricity-agreement debate to the winter session, decoupling it from the Bilaterals III package.
display_body: The Council of States' energy committee announced on Friday 21 August that it will not finish vetting the Switzerland–EU electricity agreement in time for the autumn parliamentary session, pushing the upper chamber's debate on that treaty into the winter session. The electricity accord is one of three new treaties — alongside food safety and health — inside the wider Bilaterals III package, the negotiated update to Switzerland's bilateral relationship with the European Union. The committee (known as Urek-S) said too many complex questions remain open and is planning extra sittings after the autumn session, which detaches the contested electricity deal from the rest of the package. The Federal Council intends to put the package to voters in four separate tranches, and after these first deliberations two or more separate referendums now look increasingly likely.
why: For anyone in Switzerland, this is about how — and how fast — the EU relationship moves forward. Splitting the electricity accord out gives its critics more room and lets voters accept the overarching framework while rejecting individual treaties, reshaping both the timeline and the referendum arithmetic of Bilaterals III.

headline: Economiesuisse drops army tax-hike backing
summary: Economiesuisse reversed its support for a VAT rise to fund the army, leaving Defence Minister Martin Pfister more isolated.
display_body: Economiesuisse — Switzerland's main business federation — has withdrawn its earlier backing for raising taxes to fund the army, a reversal reported on Friday 21 August that leaves Defence Minister Martin Pfister increasingly isolated. Having surprised observers in May by supporting a temporary rise in value-added tax (VAT) for defence, the federation changed course after the federal government sharply lifted its tax-revenue forecasts — companies, in particular, are paying more than expected. It now argues the roughly 2 billion francs a year the army needs should be found by reprioritising within the ordinary budget "without a tax increase," and without breaching the debt brake (the constitutional rule that caps federal deficits). Pfister's VAT plan had already been rejected across the spectrum in consultation — the Social Democrats, Greens, SVP and FDP all opposed it, leaving only his own Mitte party behind it — and the federation also rebuffed an FDP idea to book part of the arms spending as "extraordinary," a manoeuvre the government deems unlawful.
why: Parliament broadly agrees the army should get a fund allowed to take on temporary debt so it can buy equipment faster, but there is no consensus on how to pay for it. Losing the business lobby's cover makes an already politically toxic tax rise even less likely and pushes the fight toward finding cuts elsewhere in the federal budget.

headline: Israeli figures urge Swiss settlement trade halt
summary: Around 20 Israeli public figures wrote to Swiss President Guy Parmelin urging Switzerland to end trade with West Bank settlements.
display_body: A group of around 20 Israeli public figures wrote to Swiss President and Economics Minister Guy Parmelin on Friday 21 August, urging Switzerland to halt trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The signatories — among them veteran diplomat Alon Liel, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, former Knesset speaker Avraham Burg, and former Meretz party leader Zehava Gal-On — asked Bern to end commercial ties with the settlements, invoking the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion (its non-binding legal guidance) that Israel's occupation of the West Bank is unlawful; similar letters went to France, Germany and Britain. Liel stressed that the appeal is distinct from the BDS movement, which seeks a boycott of Israel itself: "We are not calling for a boycott of Israel… we are Israeli patriots," he said, casting pressure on the settlements as "a measure for Israel, not against it" and meant to push the country back toward negotiations with the Palestinians. He argued Switzerland so far does "not nearly enough."
why: The letter lands as Switzerland faces the same question after seven Western governments condemned Israel's E1 settlement plan on 20 August, and it is notable precisely because it comes from Israelis — framing a halt to settlement trade as compliance with international law rather than as hostility to Israel, and putting direct pressure on Parmelin's economics department, which oversees Swiss trade policy.
